why_use_this: Most matrices that show up in real graph, PDE, and large-linear-system code are mostly zeros -- a graph's adjacency matrix has one entry per edge, not one per pair of nodes; a finite-difference/finite-element discretization matrix has a handful of nonzero entries per row, not one per grid point in the whole domain. Storing that as a dense `Vec<f64>` of length `n_rows * n_cols` (what [vani-matrix](https://github.com/enthusiasticgeek/vani-matrix) does) wastes memory and time proportional to the *zeros* you're not using -- both memory and every operation's cost scale as `O(n^2)`/`O(n^3)` regardless of how sparse the real data is. Reach for vani-sparse instead of vani-matrix once your matrix's nonzero count (`nnz`) is much smaller than `n_rows * n_cols`: every operation here costs roughly `O(nnz)` instead, so a matrix too large to even allocate densely can still be built (via `SparseCOO`) and operated on (via `SparseCSR`) in the format built for exactly this shape of data. If you're not sure whether your matrix is sparse enough to bother, `sparse_csr_nnz(m)` compared against `m.n_rows * m.n_cols` answers that directly.

math_notes.sparse_csr_matvec: \( y = Ax \) -- the sparse matrix-vector product. For an \( n_\text{rows} \times n_\text{cols} \) matrix \( A \) and a length-\( n_\text{cols} \) vector \( x \), \( y_i = \sum_{j} A_{ij} x_j \), but the sum only ever touches the nonzero entries of row \( i \) (via `col_idx`/`vals` between `row_ptr[i]` and `row_ptr[i+1]`), not every \( j \) from \( 0 \) to \( n_\text{cols}-1 \) -- that's the whole reason this costs \( O(\text{nnz}) \) instead of \( O(n_\text{rows} \cdot n_\text{cols}) \) the way a dense `mat_vec_mul` would.
math_notes.sparse_csr_matmul: \( C = AB \) -- sparse matrix-matrix product, computed row-by-row via Gustavson's algorithm: row \( i \) of \( C \) is \( C_{i,:} = \sum_{k \in \text{nz}(A_{i,:})} A_{ik} \cdot B_{k,:} \), accumulated into a dense length-\( n_\text{cols} \) scratch row and reset after each output row -- so this implementation's per-row cost includes an \( O(n_\text{cols}) \) reset on top of the sparse accumulation itself (see the README's Gustavson's-algorithm note).
math_notes.sparse_csr_add: \( C = A + B \), entrywise, computed by merging each row's sorted (col_idx, val) pairs from \( A \) and \( B \) (matching column indices sum their values; a column present in only one operand copies through unchanged).
math_notes.sparse_csr_transpose: \( (A^T)_{ij} = A_{ji} \) -- swaps the role of row and column for every nonzero entry, then re-sorts each output row by column index to preserve the CSR sorted-within-row invariant every other operation in this package relies on.
math_notes.sparse_csr_scale: \( B = sA \), i.e. \( B_{ij} = s \cdot A_{ij} \) for every nonzero entry -- the sparsity pattern (which entries are nonzero) is unchanged; only the values are scaled.
math_notes.sparse_csr_diagonal: Returns the length-\( \min(n_\text{rows}, n_\text{cols}) \) vector \( d \) with \( d_i = A_{ii} \) -- diagonal entries that happen to be structurally absent (never pushed via sparse_coo_push) come back as \( 0.0 \), same as any other absent CSR entry.
